Vision-SL: Teaching Sign Language With Browser Hand Tracking

Oct 28, 2026 · 4 MIN READ · · BRANDON T. BANDE

  • ai
  • developers
  • zimbabwe

Hi,

I'm Brandon.

In the last article I promised to go a bit more technical on the sign language assistant. Full disclosure again: Vision-SL is not my project. It belongs to a mentee, and I am the shortcut developer who kept asking annoying questions. So this is the design as I understand it, and the thinking that got us here.

The problem, restated

We wanted a tool that teaches sign language, and we had two blockers. There is very little data on Zimbabwe Sign Language to train a model on, and none of us knew what it looks like. A classic image classifier needs thousands of labelled photos per sign. We had neither the photos nor the labels.

Stop looking at pixels

A webcam frame is a wall of pixels, and most of them have nothing to do with the sign: the wall behind you, the lighting, your sleeve, the fact that you are sitting in a room in Gweru. A model trained on raw frames has to learn to ignore all of that, which is exactly why it needs so much data.

So we stopped feeding it pictures. MediaPipe's hand landmarker finds a hand in a frame and returns 21 landmarks: the wrist, and the joints and tips of each finger. Every landmark comes with x, y and z values. That is the representation learning idea from the last article in practice: thousands of pixels of layered information collapse into 21 points that describe the shape of the hand and nothing else.

Why it runs in the browser

MediaPipe runs entirely in the browser, and that single fact quietly solved several problems at once:

  • Privacy. The student's camera feed never has to leave their device. Only coordinates are used.
  • Payload. Twenty-one points are tiny compared to video. That matters when your users pay for data.
  • Latency. There is no round trip to a server before the student gets feedback.
  • Cost. No GPU server to rent and keep alive.

From a hand to a sign

Once a hand is 21 points, comparing signs becomes a geometry problem instead of a vision problem. The first plan was simple: record a reference sign as coordinates, and when a student signs the same letter, find the closest match. Raw positions on screen would be a poor comparison, though. A hand held close to the camera and the same hand held far away are the same sign. So the sensible move is to describe the hand relative to itself, measuring the points against the wrist and scaling for hand size, so that position in the frame and distance from the camera stop mattering.

What we found interesting is how little it takes. With 3 sets of coordinates, the assistant could confidently map out a saved sign. And with as few as five signs, we could train a model on the vectors that gave feedback when evaluating a student's attempt. A small, clean representation lets a tiny dataset go a long way.

What the proof of concept could do

The first version could detect gang signs. Honestly, those were the only signs we could spell. We had no idea what Zimbabwe Sign Language looked like, so we trained on what we knew. It proved the pipeline worked end to end: camera, landmarks, comparison, feedback. It did not prove we had the right signs.

That is where the researchers came in. With their help we could train on real signs, and they brought up things we had not factored in at all.

Where it breaks

I will repeat what I said last time: just because it works doesn't mean it works the way it should.

  • Motion. A set of coordinates from a single frame describes a still hand. Many signs are movements, and a snapshot cannot capture them. That needs sequences of frames, not one.
  • Faces and bodies. Facial expression carries meaning in sign language, and hands alone miss it.
  • Real data. A representation is a clever shortcut, not a replacement. For some signs we still need real recordings from real signers, ideally with the community that uses the language.

The takeaway

If you are building with little data, change what you feed the model before you go hunting for more of it. Twenty-one clean numbers beat a million noisy pixels. Reframe the problem, find a tool that already does the heavy lifting, and run it as close to the user as you can.

Next up, I will talk about the Shona corpus, and why cleaning a pile of words turned out to be harder than collecting it.

Kudos.
